title: Adjectives and comparison
goal: Describe things and people, then compare them — with three degrees of comparison built entirely from helper words, plus one Javanese habit English lacks: repeating a word to change its meaning.
bekal: putting the adjective after its noun

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Milih kamar kos
dialogs.intro: Ahmad, Dian's friend from Jakarta, has just arrived in Yogyakarta and is looking for a *kos* (a rented room in a boarding house). Dian goes with him to see two rooms. A ngoko conversation full of adjectives and comparisons.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Kamar sing endi sing luwih apik, Yan?
lines.literal: room which which more good, Yan?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Sing ndhuwur luwih amba, nanging luwih panas.
lines.id: The upstairs one is more spacious, but hotter.
lines.literal: which upstairs more spacious, but more hot.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Rada ciyut, ning adhem lan luwih sepi.
lines.id: A bit narrow, but cool and quieter.
lines.literal: rather narrow, but cool and more quiet.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ora. Sing ndhuwur luwih larang satus èwu tinimbang sing ngisor.
lines.id: No. The upstairs one is a hundred thousand more expensive than the downstairs one.
lines.literal: no. which upstairs more expensive hundred thousand than which downstairs.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Wah, larang tenan. Sing paling murah ing kéné pira?
lines.id: Wow, that's really expensive. How much is the cheapest one here?
lines.literal: wow, expensive truly. which most cheap at here how-much?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Wolung atus, nanging cilik banget lan ora ana jendhélané.
lines.id: Eight hundred, but it's very small and has no window.
lines.literal: eight hundred, but small very and not exist window-its.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Ya wis, tak jupuk sing ngisor waé. Sing penting adhem.
lines.id: All right, I'll take the downstairs one. The main thing is it's cool.
lines.literal: yes already, I take which downstairs just. which important cool.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Pilihan sing pinter. Kamar panas kuwi angèl diturokké.
lines.id: A smart choice. A hot room is hard to sleep in.
lines.literal: choice which smart. room hot that hard slept-in.

notes: **Ning** is the short form of *nanging* (but), and you will hear it far more often. In krama it is also *nanging*. A more formal synonym: *ananging* (used in writing).
**Tenan** means "truly, really" and is used exactly like *banget*, but with a more surprised tone: *larang tenan* (really expensive). The krama is *saèstu*.
**Sing penting** — "the main thing is". Very often used to wrap up a decision, just like "what matters is…" in English.
**Angèl diturokké** — a passive form with the suffix *-ké*, covered in unit 18. For now, just notice it: the adjective *angèl* (hard) followed by a passive verb, like "hard to sleep in".
**Pinter** means "clever, smart"; the krama is also *pinter*. Its opposite is *bodho* (stupid). To praise someone's choice or action, *pinter* works just like "smart" in English.

grammars.title: Three degrees of comparison
body: Javanese builds comparison entirely with helper words, so all you need is the vocabulary — and you already know some of it.

head: Degree
Ngoko
Krama
Example
rows: *padha karo iki* — the same as this

after: **Banget comes after** the adjective, not before: *gedhé banget*, not *banget gedhé*. This is the reverse of *rada*, which comes before: *rada gedhé*.

**Tinimbang** is also often said *ketimbang* or shortened to *timbang*. All three are correct. In simple comparisons it is often dropped altogether: *sing ndhuwur luwih larang* is clear enough if the other item has already been mentioned.

**Javanese never changes the adjective itself** to compare — there is nothing like *big → bigger → biggest*. Everything is done with helper words before or after it, like English *more* and *most* but for every adjective.

blocks.text: Adjectives come **after** their noun: *omah gedhé* (big house), *kamar cilik* (small room), *wong apik* (good person). This is the opposite of English.

sections.title: Repeating words: a Javanese habit that changes meaning

blocks.text: English almost never repeats words to make new meanings. Javanese does it constantly, and the meaning shifts with the pattern. At A1 you only need to recognize the four patterns below.

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: to stroll, to go out for fun
to tidy up, to clean up
toy house (a pretend or imitation house)
to walk back and forth, to pace about
on and off, again and again
just a little at a time

blocks.text: The **vowel change** pattern — *mloka-mlaku*, *bola-bali* (back and forth), *mota-mati* — is the most distinctively Javanese and the least predictable. The vowel in the first half becomes *a*, and the result means "over and over, back and forth". You don't need to build these yourself at A1; just recognize them when you hear them.

blocks.title: Plurals: often not needed at all
items: Javanese **does not have to mark the plural**. *Aku duwé buku* can mean one book or ten books. If the number matters, say it: *buku telu*.
For an unspecified plural, use *akèh* (many) or *padha* before the verb: *bocah-bocah padha dolan* — the children (all of them) are playing.

Repeating a noun does **not** automatically make it plural in Javanese. *Omah-omah* can mean "houses", but *omah-omah* also means "to set up a household, to marry". Context tells them apart — a good example of why repeated words are best copied from real usage, not built yourself.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order to make comparisons.

items: This room is more spacious than that one.
How much is the cheapest one?
The house is big and clean.
